citation.title: Combining List Experiment and Direct Question Estimates of Sensitive Behavior Prevalence
citation.venue: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 2, p. 46 (PDF p. 4)] Suppose we have a random sample of $n$ subjects independently drawn from a large population. Let $X_i = 1$ if subject $i$ engages in a sensitive behavior and $X_i = 0$ otherwise. We attempt to measure the behavior $X_i$ using two methods: direct questioning and list experimentation. Our goal is to identify the prevalence of the sensitive behavior in the population, $\mu = \Pr[X_i = 1]$. Let $Y_i$ be the report of subject $i$ to the direct question. We assume that, under direct questioning, subjects may lie and claim that they do not engage in the behavior but will not lie and falsely claim that they do engage in the behavior. [Assumption 1: p. 46] Assumption 1 (Monotonicity). There exist three latent classes of respondents under direct questioning: those who do not engage in the behavior and report truthfully ($X_i = 0$, $Y_i = 0$), subjects who engage and report truthfully ($X_i = 1$, $Y_i = 1$), and subjects who engage but report that they do not, i.e., withhold ($X_i = 1$, $Y_i = 0$). [Direct response: p. 46] Let $p = \Pr[Y_i = 1 \mid X_i = 1]$ be the probability of a subject reporting truthfully to the direct question, given that he or she engages in the sensitive behavior. The response of subject $i$ is $Y_i = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{with probability } 1 - \mu + \mu(1 - p) \\ 1 & \text{with probability } \mu p. \end{cases}$ [p. 47 (PDF p. 5)] The probability that subject $i$ engages in the behavior, given a negative response, is therefore $\Pr[X_i = 1 \mid Y_i = 0] = \frac{(1 - p)\mu}{1 - \mu p}$. While direct questioning is sufficient to reveal $\Pr[Y_i = 1] = \mu p$, it is not sufficient to identify $\Pr[Y_i = 0 \mid X_i = 1] = 1 - p$. [List experiment: p. 47] Suppose we have a treatment $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$. In the list experiment, treated subjects ($Z_i = 1$) receive a number of control questions and an additional question about the sensitive behavior. We denote the number of items that the subject states are applicable with $V_i$. [Assumption 2: p. 47] Assumption 2 (No Liars and No Design Effects). Reframing Imai’s (2011) formulations, we observe $V_i = W_i + X_i Z_i$, where $W_i$ is the baseline outcome (under control) for subject $i$ for the list experiment. [Assumption 3: p. 47] We further require that the treatment assignment be independent of the actual behavior, direct question, and baseline response. This is a stricter variant of Imai’s (2011) ignorability assumption. Assumption 3 (Treatment Independence). $(W_i, X_i, Y_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$. [Assumption 4: p. 47] To ensure that all target quantities are well defined (and, later, to facilitate inference), we impose the mild regularity condition that all population variances are positive. Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions). $\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = y] > 0$, for $z, y \in \{0, 1\}$, $\mathrm{Var}[Z_i] > 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}[Y_i] > 0$. [Estimators: Section 3, p. 48 (PDF p. 6)] Define the sample means: $\bar Y = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i$, $\bar V_{1,0} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i Z_i (1 - Y_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i (1 - Y_i)}$ and $\bar V_{0,0} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i (1 - Z_i)(1 - Y_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i)(1 - Y_i)}$. Define an estimator of $\mu$ based on (1), $\hat\mu = \bar Y + (1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0})$. Let $\gamma = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$ be the probability of receiving the treatment question in the list experiment. [Standard estimator: p. 49 (PDF p. 7)] $\hat\mu_S = \bar V_1 - \bar V_0$, where $\bar V_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i}$ and $\bar V_0 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i (1 - Z_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i)}$. [Not printed as assumptions, but used throughout] The paper states the sampling model only as 'a random sample of $n$ subjects independently drawn from a large population'; its proofs treat $(W_i, X_i, Y_i, Z_i)$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, as independent and identically distributed, with $Z_i$ part of the draw and $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = \gamma$ (in the application, p. 53 (PDF p. 11): 'All randomizations used Bernoulli random assignment with equal probability 0.5'). $V_i$ is a count of items on a fixed finite list and is therefore bounded; no moment condition is printed. Assumption 1 is used in the form $Y_i \le X_i$ (no subject has $X_i = 0$, $Y_i = 1$). The subgroup means are ratios, and the paper assigns them no value when a $(Z, Y)$ cell of the sample is empty (P019-E003). Printed page numbers are PDF page numbers plus 42. Appendices C to F are in the online supplement (author-appendix.pdf, 7 pp.), not in the article PDF.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Appendix C, the simulated design effect (“ceiling effect”) and the design-effect clause of the 80% power sentence, as printed; Figure A1, lower-left panel
canonical_claim.location: Online supplement (author-appendix.pdf) p. 2, Appendix C, second paragraph and footnote 1; p. 3, first paragraph and Figure A1, lower-left panel 'Violated assumption: no design effects'. Not in main.pdf; the main-text counterpart is Section 4.1, last paragraph, pp. 50–51 (PDF pp. 8–9)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [Supplement p. 2, Appendix C, second paragraph] Control list responses were drawn from a binomial distribution with a success probability of 0.4 and four trials. For those units who do meet the assumptions of No False Confessions, No Liars, or No Design Effects, treatment list responses were set equal to the control list response plus one. The treatment list responses for Liars and False Confessors were set equal to their control list responses. The treatment list response for Design Affected subjects was generated as a “ceiling effect”: the control list plus one, except for those with a “4” on the control list; those units’ treatment list response remained equal to 4.$^1$ [Footnote 1] This is one of many possible design effects; the power of our test to detect any particular design effect depends on the manner in which it changes subjects’ treatment list responses. [Supplement p. 3] When approximately 20% of a sample of 800 confessors falsely confess, lie on the treatment list, or change their responses to the non-sensitive items on the treatment list, the placebo test achieves 80% power. [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $W \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$ be a subject's control list response. For a Design Affected subject who engages in the behavior, answers “Yes” and does not lie on the list, the printed rule gives the treatment list response $V_{\mathrm{printed}}(1) = \min(W + 1, 4)$. The simulator that produced Figure A1 gives such a subject $V_{\mathrm{coded}}(1) = \min(W + 1, 4) + 1$. (i) [The two response rules differ] On $W = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ the printed rule takes the values $1, 2, 3, 4, 4$ and the simulated rule the values $2, 3, 4, 5, 5$; an unaffected subject of the same kind has $W + 1$, that is $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$. At $W = 0$ the printed response is 1 and the simulated response is 2. At $W = 4$ the printed response 'remained equal to 4' and the simulated response is 5. (ii) [Population contrasts at the advertised cell] Let $W \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(4, 2/5)$, so that $\Pr[W = w] = \binom{4}{w}(2/5)^w(3/5)^{4 - w}$ equals $\frac{81}{625}, \frac{216}{625}, \frac{216}{625}, \frac{96}{625}, \frac{16}{625}$ for $w = 0, \ldots, 4$. Suppose every subject with $Y = 1$ engages in the behavior and does not lie on the list (no false confessors, no liars), is Design Affected with probability $\rho = \frac{1}{5}$ independently of $W$, reports $V = W$ when $Z = 0$, and reports $W + 1$ when $Z = 1$ if unaffected; and suppose $Z$ is independent of $W$ and of affected status. Then $\beta = E[V \mid Z = 1, Y = 1] - E[V \mid Z = 0, Y = 1]$ equals $1 - \rho \Pr[W = 4] = 1 - \frac{1}{5}\cdot\frac{16}{625} = \frac{3109}{3125} = 0.99488$ under the printed rule, and $1 + \rho\,(1 - \Pr[W = 4]) = 1 + \frac{1}{5}\cdot\frac{609}{625} = \frac{3734}{3125} = 1.19488$ under the simulated rule. The departure from the null value $\beta = 1$ of Placebo Test I is $-\frac{16}{3125}$ under the printed ceiling rule and $+\frac{609}{3125}$ under the rule that generated the panel; the two values of $\beta$ differ by exactly $\rho = \frac{1}{5}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Placebo Test I: Section 4.1, p. 50 (PDF p. 8)] Define $\beta = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$. Consider estimators $\hat\beta = \bar V_{1,1} - \bar V_{0,1}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta] = \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i Y_i} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i) Y_i}$. The paper does not write out $\bar V_{1,1}$ and $\bar V_{0,1}$; by analogy with $\bar V_{1,0}$ and $\bar V_{0,0}$ (p. 48) they are the sample means of $V_i$ among subjects with $(Z_i, Y_i) = (1, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$, and $\hat\sigma^2(\cdot)$ denotes the sample variance (p. 49). [Simulation design: supplement p. 2] 'We vary the following five quantities: the number of subjects who answer “Yes” to the direct question ($N_{\mathrm{Yes}}$, or $\sum_{i=1}^{N} Y_i$) the variability of responses to the non-sensitive list items, the proportion of $N_{\mathrm{Yes}}$ who falsely confess, the proportion of $N_{\mathrm{Yes}}$ who lie when given the treatment list, and the proportion of $N_{\mathrm{Yes}}$ whose responses to the non-sensitive list items change when given the treatment list.' 'On the x-axis of the first three panels, we vary the proportion of those subjects whose response profile violates one of the assumptions: No False Confessions, No Liars, or No Design Effects, respectively. The proportion of units that violate the other two assumptions was fixed at 0.' 'We conducted 1,000 simulations of each combination.' 'No False Confessions' is the supplement's name for Monotonicity (Assumption 1). [Simulator: deposited code, ACCG_list_source.R] Lines 82–86: design_affector(x) returns x + 1 where x != 4 and x where x == 4. Lines 103–106: V0 <- rbinom(N, size=4, prob=baseline_binomial_prob); V1 <- V0 + Ystar*(1-listliar); V1[designaffected==1] <- design_affector(V0[designaffected==1]) + Ystar[designaffected==1]*(1-listliar[designaffected==1]). In the third panel (ACCG_list_placebo_I_power.R) there are no false confessors, no list liars, 200 withholders, 200 innocents and baseline_binomial_prob = 0.4; the affected units are a uniformly drawn subset of floor(N * proportion) of all N subjects, so that with 800 admitters N = 1200 and exactly 240 units, one-fifth, are affected at proportion 0.20; half of the N subjects are treated, drawn uniformly.
canonical_claim.note: Rated Moderate (ratings.json). The instance has explicit numbers and is checked by the validator in exact rational arithmetic (check_exact.py, exact_output.txt and response_map.csv, beside the derivation); the same check gives $E[W] = \frac{8}{5}$, $\mathrm{Var}[W] = \frac{24}{25}$, and the variance of the treatment response among “Yes” respondents as $\frac{9184744}{9765625}$ under the printed rule and $\frac{10667244}{9765625}$ under the simulated rule. For general $\rho \in [0, 1]$, $\beta_{\mathrm{printed}} = 1 - \frac{16}{625}\rho$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{coded}} = 1 + \frac{609}{625}\rho$. What the instance refutes is the printed description as an account of the mechanism behind the lower-left panel of Figure A1, and with it the design-effect clause of the 80% sentence as a statement about the printed ceiling rule. The power values themselves are Monte Carlo estimates and are not formal targets: the validator's 20,000 replications at 800 admitters and 20% affected give 0.05070 (Monte Carlo standard error 0.00155) under the printed rule and 0.77965 (0.00293) under the simulated rule. Nothing here shows that power under the printed rule stays near 0.05 for every proportion or sample size: $\beta_{\mathrm{printed}} \ne 1$ for every $\rho > 0$, so the test is consistent against it. The corrected description is P019-T2 and the printed statement is P019-T16.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Appendix C, description of the simulated design effect and the design-effect clause of the 80% power sentence, corrected
canonical_claim.location: Online supplement (author-appendix.pdf) p. 2, Appendix C, second paragraph; p. 3, first paragraph and Figure A1, lower-left panel
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement. Sol's smallest repair: 'Correct the Appendix C description to say that an affected subject increases the non-sensitive count by one unless it is already four, and the sensitive item is then added. For truthful admitters the resulting total is W+2 for W<4 and 5 for W=4. Scope the 80% statement to that simulated positive design effect.'] [Hypotheses] Control list responses $W$ are drawn from a binomial distribution with a success probability of 0.4 and four trials. Every subject who answers “Yes” engages in the behavior and does not lie on the treatment list (the proportions of false confessors and of liars are fixed at 0). A subject who answers “Yes” is Design Affected with probability $\rho \in [0, 1]$, independently of $W$. Treatment $Z$ is assigned independently of $W$ and of Design Affected status. Under control every subject reports $V = W$. [Statement] The treatment list response of an unaffected subject who answers “Yes” is $W + 1$. The treatment list response of a Design Affected subject who answers “Yes” is the non-sensitive count increased by one unless it is already four, plus one for the sensitive item: $V(1) = \min(W + 1, 4) + 1$, that is $W + 2$ for $W < 4$ and $5$ for $W = 4$. Hence $V(1) - W = 1 + \mathbf{1}\{\text{affected}\}\,\mathbf{1}\{W < 4\}$ for a subject who answers “Yes”, and $\beta = E[V \mid Z = 1, Y = 1] - E[V \mid Z = 0, Y = 1] = 1 + \rho\,(1 - \Pr[W = 4]) = 1 + \frac{609}{625}\rho$, which is greater than the null value 1 for every $\rho > 0$ and equals $\frac{3734}{3125} = 1.19488$ at $\rho = \frac{1}{5}$. The power sentence is restricted to this mechanism: when approximately 20% of a sample of 800 confessors are affected in this way, the placebo test achieves about 80% power. [For comparison, the rule as printed] If instead $V(1) = \min(W + 1, 4)$ for a Design Affected subject, then $V(1) - W = 1 - \mathbf{1}\{\text{affected}\}\,\mathbf{1}\{W = 4\}$ and $\beta = 1 - \rho \Pr[W = 4] = 1 - \frac{16}{625}\rho$, which equals $\frac{3109}{3125} = 0.99488$ at $\rho = \frac{1}{5}$; the two values of $\beta$ differ by exactly $\rho$.

canonical_claim.note: The repair corrects the description to the mechanism that was simulated; it adds no assumption and changes no formula of the test. The validator records an alternative repair that keeps the printed ceiling rule ($V(1) = \min(W + 1, 4)$ with no further increment), which requires the panel to be regenerated and its power statement replaced; the evidence does not show which of the two the authors intended, and this target follows Sol's smallest repair. The exact content is the response rule and the two formulas for $\beta$, with $\Pr[W = 4] = (2/5)^4 = \frac{16}{625}$. The clause 'achieves about 80% power' is a Monte Carlo statement (the validator's estimate at 800 admitters and 20% affected is 0.77965, Monte Carlo standard error 0.00293) and has no exact formal counterpart. The main-text example on p. 50–51, 'when 20 percent of 800 subjects answering “Yes” are falsely confessing, the test has approximately 80 percent power', concerns false confessions and is not changed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Lemma 2 and the finite-sample steps of its proof and of the proof of Proposition 1 (display (6), the first equality of (9), and the sentence after (9)), as printed
canonical_claim.location: Lemma 2: p. 48 (PDF p. 6). Appendix B.1: proof of Lemma 2, displays (4)–(6), p. 62 (PDF p. 20), and (7), p. 63 (PDF p. 21); proof of Proposition 1, displays (8)–(9) and the sentence after (9), p. 63 (PDF p. 21)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Sample means and estimator: p. 48 (PDF p. 6)] $\bar Y$, $\bar V_{1,0}$, $\bar V_{0,0}$ and $\hat\mu$ as in the standing assumptions; $\gamma = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$. [Display (8): p. 63 (PDF p. 21)] The proof proceeds by working with linearized variances: $\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu] = \mathrm{Var}[1 + (1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0} - 1)] = \mathrm{Var}[(1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0} - 1)]$. (8) [Displays (4) and (5): p. 62 (PDF p. 20)] $E\left[\bar V_{1,0} \mid 1 - \bar Y = \frac{k}{n}\right] = E\left[\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n} V_j Z_j (1 - Y_j)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} Z_j (1 - Y_j)} \mid 1 - \bar Y = \frac{k}{n}\right] = E\left[\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{k} V_j Z_j}{\sum_{j=1}^{k} Z_j} \mid Y_j = 0 \text{ for } j = 1, \ldots, k\right]$, (4) and $E\left[\bar V_{1,0} \mid 1 - \bar Y = \frac{k}{n}\right] = E_Z\left[E\left[\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{k} V_j Z_j}{\sum_{j=1}^{k} Z_j} \mid Y_j = 0 \text{ for } j = 1, \ldots, k, \sum_{j=1}^{k} Z_j = i\right]\right] = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{i} E[V_j \mid Z_j = 1, Y_j = 0]}{i}\Pr\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k} Z_j = i\right)$. (5) [Display (7): p. 63] the same chain for $\bar V_{0,0}$, ending $= E[V_1 \mid Z_1 = 0, Y_1 = 0]\sum_{i=1}^{k}\Pr\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k}(1 - Z_j) = i\right) = E[V_1 \mid Z_1 = 0, Y_1 = 0]$. [Sampling model] $n$ independent draws from the population above; the events and moments in (i) to (iv) are over the joint law of the sample.
canonical_claim.note: Rated an error, Minor (ratings.json): the finite-sample steps fail as printed, while formula (3), asymptotic normality, Wald coverage and Proposition 2 hold by a first-order argument (sections 6 and 7 of the artifact). The validator's exact enumeration (check.py, check.out, exact_results.json, population.csv, count_cases.csv, beside the derivation) verifies every number above twice, once by enumerating all $9^4 = 6561$ ordered samples of the observed law and once from the six multinomial count cases on $D$; a second validator re-ran it and upheld it. Limits of the counterexample: part (i) shows that Lemma 2 is undefined as printed and false under the completion that sets empty means to 0; it does not show that every completion fails (setting an empty mean to the unknown population value $E[V \mid Z = z, Y = 0]$ restores mean independence), and Lemma 2 is true conditional on $D$ (P019-T4). Part (iii) reads the first equality of (9) as an exact identity with moments conditional on $D$; the proof announces 'linearized variances', and the equality is correct to first order: the discrepancy is $\mathrm{Cov}(A^2, h \mid D)$ with $h = s_1/N_{10} + s_0/N_{00}$, of order $n^{-2}$, with $n^2$ times it tending to $-\frac{13}{18}$ in this population. The sentence before (9) says the two subgroup means 'are uncorrelated', which is not what Lemma 2 states; that mutual uncorrelatedness holds on $D$ and still does not give the product formula. In this population the right-hand side of (3) is $\frac{7}{6}$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Lemma 2, the first equality of (9) and the sentence after (9), corrected
canonical_claim.location: Lemma 2: p. 48 (PDF p. 6). Proof of Lemma 2, displays (4)–(7): pp. 62–63 (PDF pp. 20–21). Proof of Proposition 1, displays (8)–(9) and the sentence after (9): p. 63 (PDF p. 21)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement; from Sol's smallest repair and its corrected text, with the validator's derivation, sections 2, 3, 5 and 8] [Hypotheses] $(Y_i, Z_i, V_i)$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, are independent draws from the population of Section 2 under Assumptions 1–4; $V_i$ is bounded. Let $N_{10} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i(1 - Y_i)$, $N_{00} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - Z_i)(1 - Y_i)$, $K = N_{10} + N_{00} = n(1 - \bar Y)$, $D = \{N_{10} > 0, N_{00} > 0\}$ and $\mathcal{F} = \sigma(Y_1, Z_1, \ldots, Y_n, Z_n)$. Let $m_z = E[V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = 0]$ and $s_z = \mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = 0]$ for $z = 0, 1$, $A = 1 - \bar Y$, $B = \bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0} - 1$, $b = m_1 - m_0 - 1$ and $h = \frac{s_1}{N_{10}} + \frac{s_0}{N_{00}}$. The subgroup means $\bar V_{1,0}$, $\bar V_{0,0}$ are the printed ratios on $D$; off $D$ they are given fixed bounded values (a definition, not an assumption on the population). [Statement] (a) [Empty cells] $\Pr(N_{10} = 0) = (1 - \Pr[Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0])^n > 0$ and $\Pr(N_{00} = 0) = (1 - \Pr[Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0])^n > 0$. Conditional on $K = k$, $N_{10} \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(k, \gamma)$, so the sums in (6) and (7) are $\sum_{i=1}^{k}\Pr(N_{10} = i \mid K = k) = 1 - (1 - \gamma)^k$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{k}\Pr(N_{00} = i \mid K = k) = 1 - \gamma^k$. (b) [Lemma 2, corrected] On $D$, $E[\bar V_{z,0} \mid \mathcal{F}] = m_z$ for $z = 0, 1$. Hence $E[\bar V_{z,0} \mid 1 - \bar Y, D] = m_z$, and conditional on $D$ both $\bar V_{1,0}$ and $\bar V_{0,0}$ are uncorrelated with $1 - \bar Y$: $\mathrm{Cov}(\bar V_{z,0}, 1 - \bar Y \mid D) = 0$ for $z = 0, 1$. Also $\mathrm{Cov}(\bar V_{1,0}, \bar V_{0,0} \mid D) = 0$. (c) [First equality of (9), exact form] On $D$, $E[B \mid \mathcal{F}] = b$ and $\mathrm{Var}(B \mid \mathcal{F}) = h$, and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu \mid D) = \mathrm{Var}(AB \mid D) = b^2\,\mathrm{Var}(A \mid D) + E[A^2 h \mid D]$. (d) [First equality of (9), as a linearized statement] With every moment conditional on $D$, the printed right-hand side $(E[A])^2\,\mathrm{Var}[B] + \mathrm{Var}[A]\,(E[B])^2 + \mathrm{Var}[A]\,\mathrm{Var}[B]$ equals $b^2\,\mathrm{Var}(A \mid D) + E[A^2 \mid D]\,E[h \mid D]$, and $\mathrm{Var}(AB \mid D)$ minus it equals exactly $\mathrm{Cov}(A^2, h \mid D)$. This covariance is $O(n^{-2})$, with $n^2\,\mathrm{Cov}(A^2, h \mid D) \to -2\mu p\left(\frac{s_1}{\gamma} + \frac{s_0}{1 - \gamma}\right)$; so the first equality of (9) holds with $+ O(n^{-2})$ appended, as its later lines have. (e) [Sentence after (9)] $\gamma$ is the probability of receiving treatment, so $n\gamma = E\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i\right]$; the realized count satisfies $\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i = n\hat\gamma$ with $\hat\gamma = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i / n$ (p. 49).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Sample means and estimator: p. 48 (PDF p. 6)] $\bar Y$, $\bar V_{1,0}$, $\bar V_{0,0}$, $\hat\mu = \bar Y + (1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0})$ and $\gamma = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$, as in the standing assumptions. [Display (8): p. 63 (PDF p. 21)] $\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu] = \mathrm{Var}[1 + (1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0} - 1)] = \mathrm{Var}[(1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0} - 1)]$, which rests on the identity $\hat\mu = 1 + AB$ on $D$. [Display (9), in full: p. 63] $\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu] = (E[1 - \bar Y])^2\,\mathrm{Var}[\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0}] + \mathrm{Var}[1 - \bar Y]\,(E[\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0} - 1])^2 + \mathrm{Var}[1 - \bar Y]\,\mathrm{Var}[\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0}] = (1 - \mu p)^2\,\mathrm{Var}[\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0}] + \frac{\mu p(1 - \mu p)}{n}\left(\frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}\right)^2 + \frac{\mu p(1 - \mu p)}{n}\,\mathrm{Var}[\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0}] + O(n^{-2}) = \frac{\mu p(1 - \mu)^2}{n(1 - \mu p)} + (1 - \mu p)^2\left[\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0]}{(1 - \mu p)n\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]}{(1 - \mu p)(n - n\gamma)}\right] + O(n^{-2}) = \frac{\mu p(1 - \mu)^2}{n(1 - \mu p)} + (1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0]}{n\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]}{n - n\gamma}\right] + O(n^{-2})$, (9) where $\gamma$ is the probability of receiving treatment, so $n\gamma = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i$. Multiplying by $n$ yields the desired result. [Under Assumptions 1–3] $E[1 - \bar Y] = 1 - \mu p$, $\mathrm{Var}[1 - \bar Y] = \frac{\mu p(1 - \mu p)}{n}$ and $b = m_1 - m_0 - 1 = -\frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}$ (from $m_1 - m_0 = \Pr[X_i = 1 \mid Y_i = 0] = \frac{(1 - p)\mu}{1 - \mu p}$, p. 47).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Parts (a), (b), (c) and (e) are exact for every fixed $n$, and so is the identity in (d) that $\mathrm{Var}(AB \mid D)$ minus the printed product expression equals $\mathrm{Cov}(A^2, h \mid D)$; only the order of that covariance and its limit are asymptotic. The exact steps, from section 3 of the artifact: (1) conditional on $\mathcal{F}$ the $V_i$ are independent and each has the law of $V$ given its own $(Y_i, Z_i)$ cell; (2) on $D$, $E[\bar V_{z,0} \mid \mathcal{F}] = m_z$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\bar V_{z,0} \mid \mathcal{F}) = s_z / N_{z0}$, and the two means use disjoint sets of subjects, so their conditional covariance is 0; (3) $A$ is $\mathcal{F}$-measurable, so by the law of total variance $\mathrm{Var}(AB \mid D) = \mathrm{Var}(E[AB \mid \mathcal{F}] \mid D) + E[\mathrm{Var}(AB \mid \mathcal{F}) \mid D] = b^2\,\mathrm{Var}(A \mid D) + E[A^2 h \mid D]$; (4) $\mathrm{Var}(B \mid D) = E[h \mid D]$ and $E[B \mid D] = b$; (5) $E\left[\sum_i Z_i\right] = n\gamma$. Parts (b) and (c) use only independent identically distributed sampling and positive probability of the two cells; Assumptions 1–3 enter only through the value of $b$.
canonical_claim.note: Sol's smallest repair: 'Define fixed bounded values for empty subgroup means, and for the whole plug-in variance wherever undefined. State Lemma 2 conditional on D={N10>0,N00>0} and normalize the count probabilities in its proof (or replace the proof by conditioning on all Y and Z). Before (9), specify uncorrelatedness with 1-Ybar; replace the first equality by the exact conditional total-variance identity, or append +O(n^-2) consistently with the announced linearization. Replace n*gamma=sum Z_i by n*gamma=E[sum Z_i], or delete that clause; sample counts satisfy n*gamma_hat=sum Z_i.' The repair weakens only the auxiliary lemma (to a statement conditional on non-empty cells) and qualifies one intermediate equality; the estimand, formula (3) and the asymptotic conclusions are unchanged. A bounded value on empty cells does not by itself restore the unconditional lemma (P019-T3, part (i)). With bounded completions, $n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu]$ tends to the right-hand side of (3) (section 6 of the artifact, by the influence function); that limit is the subject of P019-T18. Check in the validator's population at $n = 4$: $b = -\frac{2}{3}$, $\mathrm{Var}(A \mid D) = \frac{171}{5618}$, $E[A^2 h \mid D] = \frac{2561}{7632}$, and $\frac{4}{9}\cdot\frac{171}{5618} + \frac{2561}{7632} = \frac{141205}{404496}$, the exact variance in P019-T3.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 4.1 (Placebo Test I), the sentence on tests of distributional equality, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [p. 50 (PDF p. 8), Section 4.1, first paragraph] It is possible to jointly test the Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence assumptions. Under these assumptions, for all $t$, $\Pr[V_i = t \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] = \Pr[V_i = (t + 1) \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1]$, thus tests of distributional equality are appropriate. Any valid test of distributional equality between $V_i$ (under $Z_i = 0$, $Y_i = 1$) and $V_i + 1$ (under $Z_i = 1$, $Y_i = 1$) will permit rejection of the null. [Counterexample to the last sentence, from the validator] Let $X$, $W$, $Z$ be independent Bernoulli($\frac{1}{2}$) variables and set $Y = X$ and $V = W + XZ$ (eight atoms of probability $\frac{1}{8}$). Then $Y \le X$ (Assumption 1), $V = W + XZ$ (Assumption 2), $(W, X, Y) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$ (Assumption 3), and Assumption 4 holds: each of the four $(Z, Y)$ cells has probability $\frac{1}{4}$ and conditional variance of $V$ equal to $\frac{1}{4}$, and $\mathrm{Var}[Y] = \mathrm{Var}[Z] = \frac{1}{4}$. Given $Z = 0$, $Y = 1$, $V$ takes the values 0 and 1 with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each. Given $Z = 1$, $Y = 1$, $V$ takes the values 1 and 2 with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each, so $V + 1$ takes the values 2 and 3 with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each. The two distributions that the printed sentence compares, $V_i$ under $Z_i = 0$, $Y_i = 1$ and $V_i + 1$ under $Z_i = 1$, $Y_i = 1$, are therefore different (their supports are disjoint) although all four assumptions hold, while $V - 1$ under $Z = 1$, $Y = 1$ has the same distribution as $V$ under $Z = 0$, $Y = 1$, and the displayed identity $\Pr[V_i = t \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] = \Pr[V_i = t + 1 \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1]$ holds for all $t$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Placebo Test I: Section 4.1, p. 50 (PDF p. 8)] Define $\beta = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$. Consider estimators $\hat\beta = \bar V_{1,1} - \bar V_{0,1}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta] = \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i Y_i} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i) Y_i}$. The paper does not write out $\bar V_{1,1}$ and $\bar V_{0,1}$; by analogy with $\bar V_{1,0}$ and $\bar V_{0,0}$ (p. 48) they are the sample means of $V_i$ among subjects with $(Z_i, Y_i) = (1, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$, and $\hat\sigma^2(\cdot)$ denotes the sample variance (p. 49). In the instance $\beta = \frac{3}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = 1$, $\mu = \frac{1}{2}$ and $p = 1$.
canonical_claim.note: Rated an error, Minor: a sign misprint in the sentence, with the correct identity displayed in the sentence before it and the correct test ($\beta = 1$) used throughout. The validator's exact enumeration is in checks.py and checks_output.json (entry 'valid_model', 'placebo_distributions') beside the derivation. Read literally, the printed sentence compares control $W$ with treated $W + 2$ among “Yes” respondents, so a consistent test of that equality would reject under the null. The counterexample is to this sentence only, not to the displayed probability identity or to Proposition 3.
